prior_narrative.tldr: This thread was regrouped around speculative decoding, so it is now a run of preprints on drafting tokens cheaply and verifying them in one target pass. Nov 7-10 papers trained drafters directly on acceptance length and built block-diffusion draft trees, then Nov 13-20 work moved into serving: invalidated KV caches, looped models and grammar-constrained outputs.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 24: three papers attack the drafter itself: temperature-scaling the draft model lifts acceptance length up to ~10% at almost no cost, LEGOSpec trains swappable draft parts under matched conditions, and Pando reports 5.3x on an edge device.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Speculative decoding is a serving-side lever on decode latency and cost that leaves the target model's outputs unchanged, and this month's papers tune the parts an inference team actually owns: the drafter, the draft-tree shape, the KV cache and structured-output paths.

beats.headline: Train the drafter on acceptance length, not token accuracy
beats.summary: D-REAL and REAL Loss both argue token-level losses miss the quantity that sets the speedup: how many draft tokens survive in a row.

beats.headline: Block-diffusion drafters and smarter draft trees
beats.summary: Draft a whole block in one pass, then prune or fork the tree so verification rows are not wasted; a phrase-level drafter steps outside the target's vocabulary.

beats.headline: Speculation moves into the serving stack
beats.summary: Drafting over invalidated KV under prefill-decode disaggregation, self-speculation for looped transformers, pre-sampled verification randomness and grammar-forced tokens for JSON and tool calls.

beats.headline: Other decoding work grouped in by wording
beats.summary: Hallucination-mitigating decoding for multimodal models and model fingerprinting under sampled decoding; not speculative decoding.

beats.headline: Back to the drafter: attention, calibration, modular parts and edge trees
beats.summary: Nov 23-24 papers improve the draft side rather than the verifier, from cheap temperature scaling to a composable training framework.

open_questions: Do the reported speedups hold at production batch sizes and concurrency, where extra draft-tree rows compete for verification compute?
Does draft temperature scaling keep its ~10% acceptance gain when the target model or traffic mix changes after calibration?
Do Grammar-as-a-Draft or Callo land in a mainstream serving engine such as vLLM or SGLang beyond the authors' prototypes?
Does LEGOSpec's matched-condition comparison change which draft design (EAGLE-style, block diffusion, parallel) teams should default to?
Under the CONCOR benchmark, which published contrastive decoding methods still reduce multimodal hallucination?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you run speculative decoding, log acceptance length per route before changing anything, then try the cheapest lever first: temperature-scale your existing drafter on your own traffic, and for JSON or tool-call endpoints check whether grammar-forced tokens can fill draft rows.

day_captions.0491c6de7a511fb5: Early context: diffusion LMs commit several tokens per step and need a better rule for which to commit together.
day_captions.b1fe6c30c1c550df: First drafter-objective paper: D-REAL optimizes acceptance length with unbiased gradients.
day_captions.a4e942d0f147f07c: Prunes block-diffusion draft trees because every node costs a query row in target verification under concurrency.
day_captions.0aacbce5f85ac122: Builds fork-aware draft trees on DFlash-style block drafters, extending DDTree.
day_captions.d9424aebc884a5c5: Drafts phrases instead of target-vocabulary tokens, against a frozen target.
day_captions.256bf90ce51f6665: A second loss aimed at real expected acceptance length, three days after D-REAL.
day_captions.018074f62583197d: Ties speculation to agent serving: decode on invalidated KV while re-prefill runs under prefill-decode disaggregation.
day_captions.563c7d3375862838: Side branch: provenance-aware decoding against cross-modal hallucination in omnimodal models.
day_captions.a34c118cc3850b60: Self-speculative decoding for looped transformers, targeting their per-loop KV caches at long context.
day_captions.fb7e5418185abe5a: Side branch: fingerprinting which model is deployed when it is served with stochastic decoding.
day_captions.c08838a1ebaaf444: DICE pre-samples verification randomness to steer the drafter; reports throughput gains up to 24.6pp.
day_captions.b6559df505fa2a9e: Grammar-forced tokens fill draft rows for JSON, regex and tool-call outputs in vLLM and Rust runtimes on TPU v7x.
day_captions.f378fea92addc171: Side branch: CONCOR re-scores contrastive decoding by how it ranks real objects against hallucinated ones.
day_captions.f71af688b338f44d: Draft tokens attend to earlier block choices; 13-15% more committed tokens than DSpark, up to 3.37x on Qwen3.
day_captions.f5c599840c08b8e9: Noise-coupled draft-tree pruning on an edge device: 5.3x speedup and 4.2x energy reduction with a 16-node tree.
day_captions.6f4da66d69ee069e: Splits drafters into four swappable parts trained under matched conditions; its DFlux draft lifts acceptance on Qwen and Gemma.
day_captions.420b2dee4fa3c677: Latest item: post-hoc temperature scaling of the draft model raises acceptance length up to ~10% at near-zero cost.

prior_narrative.tldr: vLLM announced day-0 support for NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on Oct 15, covering image, document and video input through OpenAI-compatible serving. OrcaRouter comparisons against Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 Flash Vision Exp followed on Oct 16, and NVIDIA added speech with Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe on Oct 28.
prior_narrative.whats_new: AWS published a guide on Oct 29 for deploying Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Nemotron 3.5 now has a managed-Kubernetes deployment path on AWS alongside vLLM serving, so the decision shifts from whether you can host it to whether self-hosting beats a metered API.

status.detail: Servable on vLLM since launch day; speech added Oct 28 and an AWS EKS/HyperPod deployment guide followed Oct 29.

open_questions: Do independent benchmarks confirm the index-point gaps OrcaRouter reports against DeepSeek V4 Flash Vision Exp?
Will other clouds or inference engines besides vLLM and AWS add Nemotron 3.5 Super VL?

prior_narrative.tldr: This is a theme thread, not one event: three weeks of mostly arXiv work on what breaks when LLM agents run as a team, starting with KV-cache memory cost and workflow orchestration. It then split into two tracks: securing agents against malicious peers and data leaks, and tracing which agent caused a failure.
prior_narrative.whats_new: LatentLens (Nov 23) reports that a latent agent-to-agent interface often fails to improve accuracy and can degrade it across seven benchmarks, the same day REPA modeled how one agent's local errors cascade into system failure.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Multi-agent reliability now has concrete failure models (error propagation, malicious feedback during replanning, cross-agent data leaks), so a single end-to-end success rate no longer tells you why your agent team fails.

beats.headline: Running agents as a team hits memory and orchestration limits
beats.summary: Simultaneously resident KV caches become a memory bottleneck, and harnesses that spawn worker agents get an executable orchestration benchmark.

beats.headline: Malicious peers and data leaks become the threat model
beats.summary: Private retrieval and inference, an open-source leak tester, secure aggregation rules, and a replanning step hardened against hostile agent feedback.

beats.headline: Research shifts to blaming the right agent for a failure
beats.summary: Failure attribution traces the decisive error step and responsible agent; TRACE-MAS adds repair for collaboration failures in messages and task dependencies.

beats.headline: Error cascades get a model, and latent interfaces a negative result
beats.summary: REPA links local agent errors to system-level failure; LatentLens finds the latent interface frequently does not help.

beats.headline: Ranking and recommender papers clustered on shared wording
beats.summary: LLM ranking at LinkedIn scale and uncertainty signals for LLM recommenders sit outside the multi-agent theme.

open_questions: Does REPA's error-propagation model hold beyond the three Qwen base models it was evaluated on?
Does LatentLens's degradation result hold on model families other than Qwen3?
Do CoLFA or TRACE-MAS ship tooling that attributes failures in production agent traces, not only benchmark logs?
Does Kaer's protected replanning hold up on benchmarks other than its own Cintra suite?
Do any of these benchmarks release harnesses that teams adopt for their own regression evals?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Log each agent's messages and intermediate outputs per step in your multi-agent runs, because failure attribution and error-propagation methods like CoLFA and REPA need per-agent traces, not just the final answer.

prior_narrative.tldr: This is a research trend, not one event: six unrelated arXiv papers in ten days each build an agent benchmark from real sessions, real tools or real fixes. It began with group-assistant memory (Nov 3), added MCP hallucinations and memory poisoning, then moved to long-horizon infra work, researcher workspaces and privacy-aware code review (Nov 13).
prior_narrative.whats_new: The newest member (Nov 16) is a quantum recurrent-network benchmark for time-series prediction; it shares only the word "benchmarking", so PrivacyPR (Nov 13) remains the last agent-relevant entry.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Each agent paper argues that standalone task scores overstate how agents behave on stateful, tool-heavy, long-horizon or compliance-sensitive work, which is the work platform teams actually deploy them on.

beats.headline: Group-assistant benchmark tests memory use, not just recall
beats.summary: Evaluates whether an assistant shared by many users turns remembered context into appropriate help when there is no fixed answer.

beats.headline: MCPHallu and MemoryDojo benchmark how agents break
beats.summary: One measures reasoning, execution and memory hallucinations in MCP tool use; the other tests whether malicious instructions persist through agent memory across sessions.

beats.headline: Infrathon and ARE-bench test agents on sustained real work
beats.summary: One asks whether agents keep improving real AI infrastructure over long horizons; the other scores research agents inside real researcher sessions and workspaces.

beats.headline: PrivacyPR targets privacy defects in agent code review
beats.summary: A dataset linking real privacy fixes to the defects they repaired, aimed at coding agents that review pull requests.

beats.headline: Quantum RNN time-series benchmark joins on a shared keyword
beats.summary: Quantum machine-learning research with no agent or platform angle; clustered here only by the word "benchmarking".

open_questions: Will any of these benchmarks publish a public leaderboard with frontier-model scores?
Which MCP hallucination type in MCPHallu do current agents fail most often: reasoning, execution or memory?
Does MemoryDojo show poisoned memory surviving into later sessions for the memory systems teams actually ship?
Do agents that score well on standalone suites rank lower on Infrathon or ARE-bench, as the authors suggest?
What share of PrivacyPR's real privacy defects do current coding-agent reviewers catch?
Will the datasets and harnesses be released openly enough to rerun as internal evals?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If your agents persist memory or call MCP tools, add an eval that replays a poisoned instruction across sessions and logs tool-call hallucinations; keep gating rollouts on one eval built from your own logged sessions, not public scores alone.

prior_narrative.tldr: Speculative decoding research in late summer split between new drafters (diffusion draft trees) and context-heavy agent workloads (AsymSpec). Early November papers then went after the drafter itself: per-token reconsideration, block-diffusion fork trees, phrase-level drafting, and two losses that train directly for acceptance length.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Callo (Nov 13) and LoopCache (Nov 18) move the thread to serving: Callo starts decoding agent requests whose KV cache was invalidated before re-prefill finishes, and LoopCache adapts self-speculation to looped Transformers' per-loop caches.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: For agent serving, the gap now named in papers is not draft quality alone but long or edited context, where KV-cache invalidation and re-prefill stall decoding under prefill-decode disaggregation.

beats.headline: Three papers rework how the drafter proposes tokens
beats.summary: Parallel reconsideration gives the drafter a second guess per token, DForkTree builds fork-aware trees from block-diffusion drafters like DFlash, and a phrase-level drafter proposes beyond the target's own vocabulary on a frozen target.

beats.headline: D-REAL and REAL Loss train drafters directly on expected acceptance length
beats.summary: Both argue token-level training objectives miss the quantity that sets the speedup, the number of consecutively accepted draft tokens, and optimize it directly.

beats.headline: Work shifts to long-context decoding and cache-invalidated agent requests
beats.summary: A retraining-free method targets the remaining full-attention cost in hybrid linear-attention models, Callo serves cache-miss agent requests under prefill-decode disaggregation, and LoopCache handles per-loop KV caches in looped Transformers.

open_questions: Does Callo's decode-on-invalidated-KV approach ship in an open serving stack such as vLLM or SGLang, or stay a research prototype?
Do acceptance-length losses like D-REAL and REAL Loss show up in released EAGLE-3 or DFlash drafter checkpoints?
Is there a reference implementation of AsymSpec or another context-aware method that agent-pipeline builders can benchmark?
Do the November drafter gains hold when measured against production serving baselines rather than each paper's own suite?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If your agents edit context mid-session, measure re-prefill stall time on cache-miss requests before tuning drafters; drafter-level gains from these papers stay paper-only until they land in your serving stack.

prior_narrative.tldr: On Nov 2 the VIAS paper tested activation steering, adding vectors to internal activations at generation time, to make LLM agents follow several organisational values at once. A Nov 13 paper argued that steering every token pushes representations off-distribution and proposed per-token gating that follows the generation trajectory.
prior_narrative.whats_new: A Nov 19 paper argues that RL post-training of diffusion transformers amounts to activation steering, linking a costly training step to an inference-time intervention.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Activation steering is a behavior control that needs no fine-tuning run, so if it can isolate values, gate per token, or stand in for RL gains, teams get a cheaper lever for compliance and quality tuning on open-weight models.

prior_narrative.tldr: On Oct 22 an arXiv paper asked when a student trained on its own sampled outputs should follow its teacher, a refinement of on-policy distillation (OPD). By Oct 30 papers had applied OPD to multi-agent routing and to rerankers, and on Nov 8 one measured how much quantized or asynchronous rollout mismatch OPD tolerates.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 9: Agentic-OPD, an arXiv paper, argues that keeping only the best-validation checkpoint from GRPO agent training discards capabilities, and uses on-policy distillation to recover them.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: On-policy distillation is moving from a training trick into agent post-training and serving components, and its rollout cost now has a studied trade-off against quantized or asynchronous inference.
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you RL-train agents with GRPO, keep intermediate checkpoints instead of only the best-validation one until Agentic-OPD's recovery results are reproduced; none of these papers has independent replication yet.

prior_narrative.tldr: September's recursive self-improvement (RSI) papers retrained models on their own output; November's wave instead has agents rewrite their harness (prompts, tools, memory, control loop) with the base model frozen. Early November added a benchmark for that loop, a statistical-guarantee method to keep it trustworthy, and a multi-agent version for closed-loop science.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Two Nov 18 papers push RSI back into the weights: BaseRSI internalizes harness gains into a base vision-language model without training, and Piccolo co-evolves 0.8B-27B decision models with their own training data.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Harness-level RSI means an agent can change its own prompts, tools, and memory in production, so the harness itself becomes a versioned artifact that needs evals and rollback.

Do any of these loops report results outside their own benchmark harnesses?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If your agent edits its own prompts, tools, or memory, version every self-edit and gate it on a held-out eval with a rollback path before it reaches production.
